A recurrence for certain Tutte polynomials and a depth-first search conjecture

Vincent Brugidou 00footnotetext: E-mail address :vincent.brugidou@univ-lille.fr

Université de Lille, 59655 Villeneuve d’Ascq cedex, France

Abstract We combinatorially prove a recurrence between the Tutte polynomials of graphs obtained by contraction of the complete graphs KnK_{n}. This generalizes to two variables a relation previously obtained by the author between the inversion enumerating polynomials in the colored trees. A combinatorial interpretation concerning certain polynomials recently introduced by the author via the theory of symmetric functions is also conjectured . This intrepretation uses the depth-first search.

keywords : Tutte polynomial, complete graph, tree inversions, positive sequence, depth-first search.

.

1 Introduction

In [2, Eq. (6.5)], we have algebraically proven the following recurrence relation valid for integers nn and rr, such that n>r≥1n>r\geq 1 :

Jn(r)​(q)=∑s=1n−r(n−rs)​[r]qs​q(s2)​Jn−r(s)​(q).J_{n}^{\left(r\right)}(q)=\sum\limits_{s=1}^{n-r}\binom{n-r}{s}\left[r\right]_{q}^{s}\;q^{\binom{s}{2}}J_{n-r}^{\left(s\right)}(q). (1.1)

In this equation, [r]q\left[r\right]_{q} is the qq-analogue of rr and the polynomials Jn(r)J_{n}^{\left(r\right)} are special cases of the inversion enumerator polynomials in colored tree sequences introduced by Stanley [8] and Yan [9]. These latter polynomials are themselves generalizations of the polynomial Jn=Jn(1)J_{n}=J_{n}^{\left(1\right)}, which is the enumerator of inversions in trees on nn vertices, first introduced in [7]. All these polynomials also have interpretations in terms of parking functions, for which we refer to the review article [10].

In [4], it was noted that :

Jn(r)​(q)=Tn(r)​(1,q)​,J_{n}^{\left(r\right)}(q)=T_{n}^{(r)}\left(1,q\right)\text{,} (1.2)

where Tn(r)​(x,y)T_{n}^{\left(r\right)}\left(x,y\right) is the Tutte polynomial of the complete graph KnK_{n}, contracted over all edges between rr vertices of KnK_{n}. We will sometimes use the simplified notation Kn/rK_{n/r} for this contracted graph (see [3, Remark 4.5] for the explanation of this notation).

The main result of this article is the following theorem, which generalizes (1.1)\left(1.1\right) to two variables.

Theorem 1.1

the Tutte polynomial of graphs Kn/rK_{n/r} vérifies for n>r≥1n>r\geq 1 the recurrence relation :

Tn(r)​(x,y)=∑s=1n−r(n−rs)​[r]ys​y(s2)​Tn−r(s)​(x,y)+(x−1)​Tn−r(1)​(x,y)​,T_{n}^{\left(r\right)}(x,y)=\sum\limits_{s=1}^{n-r}\binom{n-r}{s}\left[r\right]_{y}^{s}\;y^{\binom{s}{2}}T_{n-r}^{\left(s\right)}(x,y)+\left(x-1\right)T_{n-r}^{\left(1\right)}\left(x,y\right)\text{,} (1.3)

where [r]y=1+y+y2+…+yr−1\left[r\right]_{y}=1+y+y^{2}+...+y^{r-1}.

This equation is proven combinatorially, using one of the classical expressions for the Tutte polynomial. It allows us to recursively compute all polynomials Tn(r)T_{n}^{\left(r\right)} (see table 1), and in particular the Tutte polynomials of complete graphs KnK_{n} since TKn=Tn(1)T_{K_{n}}=T_{n}^{\left(1\right)}.

The second part of the article concerns the polynomials Jλ​(q)J_{\lambda}\left(q\right) introduced in [3, Theorem 3.1 and Corollary 3.5] from the theory of symmetric functions. These polynomials, defined for any integer partition λ=(λ1,λ2​,…, ​λr)\lambda=\left(\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2}\text{,..., }\lambda_{r}\right), also generalize the inversions enumerator polyniomal JnJ_{n}, but in a different direction from that of the polyniomals Jn(r)J_{n}^{\left(r\right)}. In fact, we have Jn=J(n)J_{n}=J_{\left(n\right)}, where (n)\left(n\right) is the one-part partition. The JλJ_{\lambda} polynomials have coefficients in ℤ\mathbb{Z} , their order is zero and their degree is :

(n−12)+r−1−n⁡(λ)​,\binom{n-1}{2}+r-1-n\left(\lambda\right)\text{,}

where n=|λ|=λ1+λ2n=\left|\lambda\right|=\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}+…+λr\lambda_{r}, r=l⁡(λ)r=l\left(\lambda\right) is the length of λ\lambda, and n⁡(λ)=∑i=1r(i−1)​λin\left(\lambda\right)=\sum\nolimits_{i=1}^{r}\left(i-1\right)\lambda_{i}.

In [3]\left[3\right] we formulated two conjectures about the polynomials JλJ_{\lambda} :

Conjecture 1.2

The coefficients of JλJ_{\lambda} are strictly positive.

Conjecture 1.3

The sequence of coefficients of JλJ_{\lambda} is log-concave.

These two conjectures have been verified in some cases and in particular for all polynomials JλJ_{\lambda} such that |λ|=n≤43\left|\lambda\right|=n\leq 43, which represents 3756325 polynomials. Furthermore, it has been shown that the coefficients of the polynomials Jn(r)J_{n}^{\left(r\right)} of Eq. (1.1)\left(1.1\right) verify these statements. This is a heuristic argument in favor of these conjectures, since the following relations have been established between the polynomials JλJ_{\lambda} and Jn(r)J_{n}^{\left(r\right)} [3, Corollary 3.6] :

F​o​r​n≥r≥1,(n−1)!r!​(n−r)!​q(r2)​Jn(r)​(q)=∑|λ|=n,l⁡(λ)=rqn⁡(λ)m⁡(λ)!​Jλ​(q)​.For\;n\geq r\geq 1,\;\dfrac{\left(n-1\right)!}{r!\left(n-r\right)!}q^{\binom{r}{2}}J_{n}^{\left(r\right)}\left(q\right)=\sum\limits_{\left|\lambda\right|=n,\;l\left(\lambda\right)=r}\dfrac{q^{n\left(\lambda\right)}}{m\left(\lambda\right)!}J_{\lambda}\left(q\right)\text{.} (1.4)
F​o​r​n≥1,Jn+1​(q)=n​∑|λ|=nqn⁡(λ)m⁡(λ)!​Jλ​(q).For\;n\geq 1,\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\ \ \;\;J_{n+1}\left(q\right)=n\sum\limits_{\left|\lambda\right|=n}\dfrac{q^{n\left(\lambda\right)}}{m\left(\lambda\right)!}J_{\lambda}\left(q\right).\;\;\;\;\; (1.5)

In these equations, m⁡(λ)=(r1,r2,…)m\left(\lambda\right)=\left(r_{1},r_{2},...\right) is the multiplicity vector of λ=(λ1,λ2​,…, ​λr)\lambda=\left(\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2}\text{,..., }\lambda_{r}\right), that is, rjr_{j} is the number of parts of λ\lambda, equal to j∈ℕ∗j\in\mathbb{N}^{\ast} and m⁡(λ)!=r1!​r2!​…m\left(\lambda\right)!=r_{1}!r_{2}!....These notations for integer partitions are those of [6]. A third argument in favor of these conjectures comes from Corollary 5.2 of [3] which implies that for any integer partition λ\lambda, such that n=|λ|≥2n=\left|\lambda\right|\geq 2, the sequence of the last n−1n-1 coefficients of JλJ_{\lambda} is strictly positive and log-concave.

To my knowledge, no progress has been made on these conjectures since [3] and [4]\left[4\right]. An attractive way to prove Conjecture 1 would be to find a combinatorial interpretation of JλJ_{\lambda}. Analysing the proof of Theoreme 1, we conjecture in this article a combinatorial interpretation of the following polynomial where |λ|=n\left|\lambda\right|=n :

Pλ​(t)=n​tn​(1+t)n⁡(λ)m⁡(λ)!​Jλ​(1+t)​.P_{\lambda}\left(t\right)=nt^{n}\dfrac{\left(1+t\right)^{n\left(\lambda\right)}}{m\left(\lambda\right)!}J_{\lambda}\left(1+t\right)\text{.} (1.6)

To this end, we use the depth-first search introduced in [5] as a combinatorial correspondence between graph and tree. We show some cases where this interpretation is verified.

2 Notation Conventions

2.1 On Sets

If AA and BB are finite sets, |A|\left|A\right| denotes the cardinality of AA and A−B={x∈A,x∉B}A-B=\left\{x\in A,x\notin B\right\}.

2.2 On Graphs

The terminology and notations concerning graphs are, in general, those of [1]. We recall here some of these notations that are important for our subject.

Let G=(V⁡(G),E⁡(G))G=\left(V\left(G\right),E\left(G\right)\right) be a finite graph whose vertex set is V⁡(G)V\left(G\right) and whose edge set is E⁡(G)E\left(G\right). If F⊆F\subseteq E⁡(G)E\left(G\right), then G\FG\backslash F is the graph with the same vertices as GG and whose edge set is E⁡(G)−FE\left(G\right)-F. Still with F⊆F\subseteq E⁡(G)E\left(G\right), G/FG/F is the graph obtained by contraction of the edges belonging to FF. If R⊆V⁡(G)R\subseteq V\left(G\right), then G−RG-R is the graph obtained by deleting from GG the vertices belonging to RR, along with all edges incident to those vertices. If RR contains no vertices adjacent in GG, then G/RG/R is the graph obtained by replacing all the vertices in RR with a single vertex, which is incident to all the edges incident to the elements of RR.

We also adopt the author’s own notational conventions, as follows. If VV is a finite set, we denote by KVK_{V} the complete graph whose vertex set is VV. Clearly, KV≈K|V|K_{V}\approx K_{\left|V\right|}. Let V={1,2,…,n}V\mathbf{=}\left\{1,2,...,n\right\}, and R={u1,u2,…,ur}⊆VR=\left\{u_{1},u_{2},...,u_{r}\right\}\subseteq V with |R|=r\left|R\right|=r. Define R¯=V−R={w1,w2,…,wn−r}\overline{R}=V-R=\left\{w_{1},w_{2},...,w_{n-r}\right\}. In KV/E⁡(KR)≈Kn/rK_{V}/E\left(K_{R}\right)\approx K_{n/r}, we denote by 0R0_{R} the vertex that replaces, in the contraction, the rr elements of RR, and by (ui,wk)(u_{i},w_{k}) the edge incident to 0R0_{R}, coming under the contraction from the edge joining uiu_{i} to wkw_{k} in KVK_{V}. The edges joigning two vertices of R¯\overline{R} remain unchanged under contraction.

Let S={v1,v2,…​vs}⊆R¯S=\left\{v_{1},v_{2},...v_{s}\right\}\subseteq\overline{R} with |S|=s\left|S\right|=s, and contract KV/E⁡(KR)K_{V}/E\left(K_{R}\right) along the edges of KSK_{S}. We obtain the set :

(KV/E⁡(Kr))/E⁡(KS)=KV/(E⁡(KR)∪E⁡(KS)).(K_{V}/E\left(K_{r}\right))/E\left(K_{S}\right)=K_{V}/(E(K_{R})\cup E\left(K_{S}\right)).

The previous edge-notation procedure can be applied to this graph : 0S0_{S} will denote the vertex replacing the vertices belonging to SS, an edge joigning 0S0_{S} to w∈(R¯−S)w\in(\overline{R}-S) will be denoted (vj,w)(v_{j},w) and an edge joigning 0R0_{R} to 0S0_{S} will be denoted (ui,vj)(u_{i},v_{j}). The others edges remain unchanged with respect to those of KV/E⁡(KR)K_{V}/E\left(K_{R}\right).

where the sum runs over the set of spanning subgraphs HH of Kn/r≈KV/E⁡(KR)K_{n/r}\approx K_{V}/E\left(K_{R}\right), with V={1,2,…,n}V=\left\{1,2,...,n\right\} and R={u1,u2,…,ur}R=\left\{u_{1},u_{2},...,u_{r}\right\}. 4.1 Introduction of the polynomial PλP_{\lambda}

the relation (4.1)\left(4.1\right) applied to Kn/rK_{n/r}, shows that, taking (1.2)\left(1.2\right) into account :

Let us first recall how, in [5], the depth-first search associates a tree 𝒯⁡(C)\mathcal{T}\left(C\right) with each spanning connected graph of KnK_{n}. We start at vertex 11, and at each step, we go to the greatest adjacent unvisited vertex if there is one, otherwise, we backtrack. An example is given in Figure 4 for a spanning connected graph of K8K_{8}.

Definition 4.1

Then, we define w⁡(C)w\left(C\right) as the word obtained from τ⁡(C)\tau\left(C\right) by deleting 1 and all the vertices already visited (in the search order). w⁡(C)w\left(C\right) is a word of nn letters, all distinct, taken in the alphabet {2,3,…,n+1}\left\{2,3,...,n+1\right\}.

and

P(2,2)​(t)=4​t4​(1+t)2​J(2,2)​(1+t)=12​t4+32​t5+30​t6+12​t7+2​t8​.P_{\left(2,2\right)}\left(t\right)=4t^{4}\left(1+t\right)^{2}J_{\left(2,2\right)}\left(1+t\right)=12t^{4}+32t^{5}+30t^{6}+12t^{7}+2t^{8}\text{.}

Using depth-first search and the definition of 𝒫λ\mathcal{P}_{\lambda}, we manually partitioned the 288288 graphs of 𝒫4(2)\mathcal{P}_{4}^{\left(2\right)} into the two sets 𝒫(3,1)\mathcal{P}_{\left(3,1\right)} and 𝒫(2,2)\mathcal{P}_{\left(2,2\right)}. We recorded the number of edges in each of these graphs. We thus verified, for λ=(3,1)\lambda=\left(3,1\right) and λ=(2,2)\lambda=\left(2,2\right), Conjecture 4.3, namely :

∑C∈𝒫(3,1)te⁡(C)=P(3,1)​(t)​ and ​∑C∈𝒫(2,2)te⁡(C)=P(2,2)​(t)​.\sum\limits_{C\in\mathcal{P}_{\left(3,1\right)}}t^{e\left(C\right)}=P_{\left(3,1\right)}\left(t\right)\text{ and \ }\sum\limits_{C\in\mathcal{P}_{\left(2,2\right)}}t^{e\left(C\right)}=P_{\left(2,2\right)}\left(t\right)\text{.}

It is easy to see that all the other partitions such that |λ|≤4\left|\lambda\right|\leq 4, are one of the types in 1). We therefore verified Conjecture 4.3 for |λ|≤4\left|\lambda\right|\leq 4. It would be desirable, using a computer program, to verify this conjecture for |λ|>4.\left|\lambda\right|>4. In conclusion, note that Conjecture 4.3 does not a priori imply Conjecture 1.2 on the positivity of coefficients of JλJ_{\lambda}. However, we can hope that a proof of Conjecture 4.3 will provide clues to prove the latter.
